How this list is ordered

Four gates, applied in this order to every published US record. There is no score and no weighting — each gate either separates two machines or hands them to the next one.

  1. 1 Does it run the set?

    Every record is put through the compatibility engine against all of the loads at once — running watts against continuous output, the worst start-up instant against the surge ceiling, waveform where a load demands one. Green first, then the tight fits, then anything the engine could not read, then the machines that cannot do it. A machine that cannot start the load in front of it is not a cheaper option.

  2. 2 Can we prove how long?

    A runtime is only printed where the brand publishes what it takes to compute one — a usable-capacity coefficient, whether stated as depth of discharge and inverter efficiency or as one combined figure — and never from the number on the box. Records that reach the target sort first, records with a proven but shorter figure next (longest first: inside that band none of them does the job, so the one that gets closest wins), and records whose duration cannot be proven at all sort last inside their verdict band. That is a statement about published data, not about the hardware, and each of those rows says so.

  3. 3 Can it be bought today?

    A record under a verified out-of-stock policy, or one we may not sell into your state, sorts behind an equivalent one that can be bought. It stays on the list with the reason attached rather than disappearing. Whether WattPair happens to hold a purchase link for a record is not part of this gate and never moves it: a machine we cannot link to is ranked exactly as if we could, and simply carries no buy button.

  4. 4 Then price.

    Cheapest first, inside everything above. One mains standard and one currency per page, so every comparison is like for like. A record with no verified price sorts to the back of its own band — the absence of a price is not a low price.

The loads this ranks against

A single 12 V portable compressor fridge, on its own — a variable-speed DC compressor with no locked-rotor current at all, so unlike every other scenario on this site, the electrical check is not the interesting question here. What decides this list is entirely the second gate: which brands publish enough about their own battery to prove an actual number of hours, rather than a nameplate a reader could divide themselves.

Why 12 records carry no printable runtime

12 of the 12 records here start and hold this load set and still carry no runtime this page will print — not because of anything a brand did, but because we have found no duty cycle and no modulation curve published for 12V portable fridge/freezer. There is therefore no average draw to divide any battery by, for any station here, however completely that station documents its own coefficients. Why we could not find that figure for this particular load is set out above, under the duration target. That holds regardless of disclosure quality, and this page can put a number on it: 7 of the 12 records here do publish the depth of discharge and the inverter efficiency an hour figure is computed from — the same 7 that carry proven runtimes on this site's other lists — and on this load they print nothing either. The gate sits on the load, not on anyone’s battery documentation.

This page cannot even offer the fallback bound the other pages on this site print. That bound is a nameplate divided by the set’s own average draw, and the average draw is exactly what is missing — with no duty cycle to weight it by, there is nothing to divide any capacity above by, for any row here, cheap or expensive. Every capacity in the ranked list above is still each manufacturer’s own published figure; it is the arithmetic connecting it to a number of hours that cannot be done for this load.

The scope of that finding, stated: as of 2026-08-01 the manufacturer documents behind this load were read in full for a duty cycle or a modulation curve, and none exists in them. That is a statement about this ONE load record, not about the 12 stations paired with it here — each of those is judged on its own disclosure everywhere else on this site, and none of them is being marked down for it. This is a statement about published data, not about the hardware — the verdict column judges that separately, and it comes first.

The load that changes the answer

Add a Starlink Mini to the same set and the first gate is still a formality: 12 of the 12 still clear it outright, against 12 on the set above. The reason is one instant: a Starlink Mini asks for 60 W at start-up on its own, against 180 W for everything on the list above put together. That start-up figure is this unit’s own manufacturer’s. A Starlink Mini does not cost this list a single machine, because 30 W of running draw is background noise against a fridge’s own compressor — but it is not free. Every constant watt added here shortens the hours every proven figure above is good for, which is the actual cost of a second gadget on a small power budget. The quiz carries this set as a preset.

Questions people ask about this list

Do all 12 of them really run it?
On this set, yes — and that is the finding, not a formality. 90 W of running draw and 180 W at the worst start-up instant is inside every published US record's ceilings, so not one of them is ruled out on electrical grounds. Which means “will it run a 12V portable fridge/freezer” is answered yes for all 12 — but “how long” is not: not one of them carries a runtime this page can compute, so that question stays open rather than answered here.
Does it really have no start-up surge at all?
Its data sheet has no row for one — which is a different claim, and the record makes the weaker one. The compressor is a Secop BD35F/BD50F variable-speed unit; its sheet gives a maximum continuous current and a fuse specification and carries no locked-rotor column anywhere. The 180 VA above is that fuse: a DIN 7258 15 A automobile fuse at 12 V, which is the maker’s own statement of the highest current this appliance may ever pull, against a maximum published continuous current of 6.3 A. The control board ramps the motor up instead of throwing it across the line, and a start that fails is reported as an error code rather than as a stall. This is the one figure in this library inferred from a field being ABSENT from its source, and it is labelled that way on the record rather than presented as a measurement.
